summary: This note is an excerpt from the Wikipedia article on Imperial College London, covering its graduate employability and rankings, its research assessment results, its Centre for Co-Curricular Studies, and its institutional mergers and building history. It highlights job prospects and REF 2014 performance and traces the college's expansion through mergers with medical schools in 1988, 1995 and 1997.
one_line: Excerpt from the Imperial College London article on graduate job prospects, REF 2014 results, co-curricular studies, and merger history.
key_facts: As of 2014, the average starting salary of an Imperial graduate was the highest of any UK university.
The Sunday Times ranked Imperial Computing graduates as having the second highest average starting salary in the UK after graduation, over all universities and courses.
In 2012, the New York Times ranked Imperial College as one of the top 10 most-welcomed universities by the global job market.
In May 2014, Imperial was voted highest in the UK for Job Prospects by students voting in the Whatuni Student Choice Awards.
Imperial submitted 1,257 staff across 14 units of assessment to the 2014 Research Excellence Framework (REF).
In the 2014 REF results, 46% of Imperial's submitted research was classified as 4*, 44% as 3*, 9% as 2* and 1% as 1*, giving an overall GPA of 3.36.
Times Higher Education ranked Imperial 2nd overall for GPA and 8th for research power based on the REF results, compared with 6th and 7th for the RAE 2008.
The Centre For Co-Curricular Studies offers elective subjects and language courses outside science for students in other faculties and departments.
Language courses at the Centre For Co-Curricular Studies are available in French, German, Japanese, Italian, Russian, Spanish, Arabic and Mandarin Chinese.
The Centre For Co-Curricular Studies is home to the Science Communication Unit, which offers master's degrees in Science Communication and Science Media Production.
In 1988 Imperial merged with St Mary's Hospital Medical School, becoming The Imperial College of Science, Technology and Medicine.
In 1995 Imperial launched its own academic publishing house, Imperial College Press, in partnership with World Scientific.
Imperial merged with the National Heart and Lung Institute in 1995.
In 1997 Imperial merged with Charing Cross and Westminster Medical School, Royal Postgraduate Medical School (RPMS) and the Institute of Obstetrics and Gynaecology.
The Imperial College Act 1997 transferred the property of Charing Cross and Westminster Medical School, the National Heart and Lung Institute and the Royal Postgraduate Medical School to Imperial.
In 1998 the Sir Alexander Fleming Building was opened by Queen Elizabeth II to provide a headquarters for the College's medical and biomedical research.
